Anthropic’s network and Congress

450 of 533

More than four in five members of Congress have a documented tie to Anthropic’s network: the company, the funders behind it, the groups they fund, and their PACs and lobbyists. This is the public record of those ties, and of how fast they were made.

Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026. A tie is a public record that links the member and the network: a contribution, a lobbying report on the member’s bill, a fellow in the office, a statement.

Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. A tie can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. It is not an allegation, and a contribution is not a vote.

Start with the company itself.

I · The arrival

At the end of 2024, 10 members had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. Twenty-one months later: 196.

A lit dot is a member now serving who had received at least one contribution from a person who lists Anthropic as employer, or from the company’s PAC. The employees gave their own money: $25K in the first quarter of 2025, $3.2M in the third quarter of 2026. 92% of their $5.6M is dated 2026.

Source: FEC contribution records in this project’s tables: contributions to the campaign, leadership PAC or single-member joint fundraising committee of a serving member, through Sept. 30, 2026.

A person’s contribution is their own money, not their employer’s. Employer is as the giver reported it to the FEC. The record stops at Sept. 30, 2026.

Who wrote those checks?

Every contribution by an Anthropic employee to a member now serving: 1,027 of them, $5.6M

The employees’ gifts only (the PAC’s are on a later slide), through Sept. 30, 2026. The scale is logarithmic: each line is ten times the one below.

I · The arrival

Ten givers account for 58% of the employees’ dollars.

89 names (a first name and a surname) list Anthropic as their employer on these contributions; together they gave $5.6M. Half of them gave $20,500 or less. The two largest gave $553K and $545K, spread across 70 and 65 members.

Each circle is one giver; its area is what that person gave to serving members.

Givers are private individuals and are not named here. The count is of first names and surnames as filed: two people who share both would count as one.

Where did it land?

I · The arrival

Democrats received 55% of the dollars. But six of the eight members who received $100,000 or more are Republicans.

The money went to 111 Democrats and 84 Republicans. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, received the most: $218K.

Source: FEC contribution records; all years on record, through Sept. 30, 2026.

Totals are by member: campaign, leadership PAC and single-member joint fundraising committees together. A total is what the committees received, not what a member asked for.

Then the company’s own PAC began to give.

I · The arrival

Its PAC’s first gift on record is dated June 29, 2026. By September 30 it had given to 81 members.

ANTHROPAC, the company’s political action committee, made 87 gifts in those three months, $200K in all, beside the employees’ $5.6M. 57 members received a gift in September.

Source: FEC records of ANTHROPAC (Anthropic PBC’s political action committee); first gift on record in this project’s tables.

A member who received gifts in two months is counted in each month, and once in the 81.

The PAC is the small part. The large money moved another way.

II · The bigger money

Anthropic announced $40.0M for Public First Action. A super PAC that group funds reported $15.0M of independent spending for one House candidate.

Two amounts, two separate records, both from 2026: Anthropic’s announcements and the super PAC’s FEC reports. The candidate, Alexander Bores, a Democrat in NY-12, does not serve in Congress.

Three kinds of record, not one stream of dollars: an announcement (dashed), then the transfers and the independent spending the super PACs reported to the FEC (solid). Width is the amount.

Source: Anthropic’s announcements; FEC contribution and outside-spending reports of the Public First committees. Not drawn: $1.0M Public First Action passed to a third committee, and one $105K ad naming a member without saying for or against.

No filing on record lists Public First Action’s donors. A contribution does not direct spending, and the filings state the super PACs acted alone.

The company’s funders gave more, and for longer.

II · The bigger money

The network gave 26 committees $200M; they spent $541M, from all their donors, for or against members, $420M of it against Republicans.

Half of the $200M is Dustin Moskovitz’s $100M to FF PAC, of $130M on record from him to outside groups in 2016–2024. The top spender, House Majority PAC, took in $5.3M of the $200M and spent $213M.

Two separate records on one scale: no dollar is traced from a gift to an expenditure, and a contribution does not direct spending.

Source: FEC outside-spending reports naming a member now serving; the same 26 committees’ receipts on record from the network (transfers among the Public First committees counted once; $420K from those super PACs’ other donors included).

Independent spending is not coordination; a member opposed received nothing. Money in counts only gifts on record.

One kind of money reaches more members than any of this, and the network did not give it.

Who gave, and which members the committees’ spending named

II · The bigger money

No tie reaches more members: lobbyists at firms with a network client gave 323 of them $1.4M of their own money.

Each firm was registered to lobby for a client in the network when the gift was made. For 299 of the 323 members, the giver is also named on that client’s own filings.

Each lit seat is a member who received at least one such gift.

Source: lobbyists’ semi-annual contribution reports to Congress, Feb. 19, 2021 to June 30, 2026; FEC records tie each receiving committee to one member.

The money is the lobbyist’s own, not the client’s, and the record does not say why a gift was made. Counted: gifts dated while the firm was registered for a network client. Named lobbyists only: $1.2M in 994 gifts.

Lobbyists are paid to ask. Here is what Anthropic spent.

Lobbyists’ own gifts to members now serving, by election cycle

74 lobbyists at 23 firms made the 1,152 gifts: 153 Democrats, 169 Republicans and one independent received at least one. The total has grown in each cycle; for 2026, the reports read so far stop at June 30.

III · The asks

Anthropic’s reported lobbying spending is up twentyfold since 2023: $280K that year, $5.6M in the first nine months of 2026.

Beside the field the whole network is small: 0.5% of what was reported in 2025 on lobbying reports that name AI, and 2.9% on reports whose every issue is AI.

Source: quarterly lobbying reports (form LD-2) through Sept. 30, 2026, for Anthropic and the nine other network groups whose reports print an amount; for the shares, the 2019–2025 reports this project classified as naming AI or an AI bill by title, after its documented exclusions.

Amounts are as filed, rounded. The 2023 figure is outside firms’ reported income; from 2024 it is the company’s own reported expenses, which include what it paid the firms. A report’s amount covers every issue on it, so each share is of report totals, not of AI lobbying; 2025 is the last full year compared.

Small beside the field. But what did it ask about?

What was reported in 2025 on lobbying reports that name AI, at about $1M a square

1,211 squares after rounding. Six are the whole network’s: $5.6M in 2025, a different sum from the $5.6M Anthropic alone reported for January to September 2026. Each report’s amount covers every issue on it, so these are upper bounds on AI lobbying. Over 2024–25, Anthropic ($3.9M) reported less than OpenAI ($4.8M) and far less than Meta ($50.7M).

III · The asks

The three bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic are about chips. All six sponsors received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.

The gifts are a separate record, the FEC’s: $328,500 in all. No report says which way the company lobbied.

Source: the 68 quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic, 2023 to Sept. 30, 2026 (each bill described from its official title); FEC contribution records.

A report that names a bill says the client lobbied on it, not which way and not whether a sponsor’s office was contacted. The gifts are individuals’ own or the PAC’s; no gift is tied to a bill.

How often did a sponsor also receive a gift?

The four bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic

Each bill with words excerpted from its official title as introduced (Government Publishing Office bill status files), its House and Senate numbers and its sponsors now serving; each dot is one quarterly report that names it. Of the 68 reports filed for Anthropic, 18 name a bill. Annual defence and spending bills are not ranked (none is named as often as these three); House and Senate versions count as one bill where a report pairs them.

III · The asks

Lobbying reports filed for Anthropic name bills by 23 members. 19 of them received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.

Among the 91 sponsors of AI bills with no bill named in any network report, it was 47; in all of Congress, 196 of 533. Of the 23, 13 are senators, and 60 of all 100 senators received such gifts.

A report that names a bill says the client lobbied on it: not which way, and not whether the sponsor’s office was contacted.

Source: quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic, matched to verified sponsors (annual defence and spending bills not counted); AI bills from this project’s companion study; FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

No money is attributed to the lobbying; each gift is an individual’s own or the PAC’s. Which came first, a gift or a report, says nothing about why either was made. “Filed for Anthropic” means the company’s own report or one by a firm it hired.

All of this is recent. The grants are older.

The 38 members whose bills the network’s lobbying reports name

Reports filed for Anthropic name bills by 23 of them; reports filed for the network’s other groups name bills by 15 more. With both counted, 27 of the 38 received a gift from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. Each dot is one quarterly report naming a bill the member sponsored; the bar and the sum are those gifts, all years on record.

IV · The decade before

By the end of 2024, seven of the network’s funders had already granted $528M.

That is when ten members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. The grants, from 2015 on, paid for work on AI, technology, biosecurity and catastrophic risk; none names a member of Congress as its recipient. The largest grantee is Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET).

Source: IRS Form 990 grant schedules and the funders’ own published grant lists (Coefficient Giving, Survival and Flourishing Fund, Future of Life Institute).

A grant to an organisation is not money to a member. Published grant lists and tax filings can lag, so the 2025 and 2026 totals may still rise; grants approved for future years are left out.

Follow the largest grantee.

Where the grants went: the 12 largest of 276 grantees

Together these twelve hold $664M of the $932M that every funder on record has granted to 276 grantees for this work. The chart on the slide draws $931M of it: the seven largest funders’ grants dated 2015 to 2026.

IV · The decade before

The largest grantee was awarded $55.0M in January 2019. That June a House panel heard one of its witnesses.

It is Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), one of only two of the ten largest grantees with a witness on record. One witness spoke for both: Jason Matheny, as CSET’s founding director in 2020 and at least three times since as RAND’s president.

Each dot is one appearance before a committee of Congress. Ringed: the same witness, for two grantees.

Source: witness lists from congress.gov, House committee pages and Senate hearing transcripts (published months late); grants as on the previous slide.

Testifying is not lobbying, and no grant is tied to an appearance or to a person. For RAND, CNAS and Carnegie only testimony on work the network funds counts. “At least”: two more hearings where he spoke as RAND’s president are on record outside this count.

Witnesses visit. Who works inside?

IV · The decade before

The Horizon Institute, a network grantee, has funded 25 fellows inside Congress since 2022, in offices of both parties.

Horizon says fellows and hosts make their own decisions and the host manages the work. Eight of the nine senators who hosted a fellow have also received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC; so have 60 of all 100 senators.

Each dot is one placement, as the programme’s roster lists it.

Source: Horizon Institute placement pages and alumni lists, and its “Host a Fellow” and “About” pages as saved in 2026; IRS Form 990 grant schedules; FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

No gift is tied to a placement, and a gift is the giver’s own money. With the one House host it is nine of ten serving hosts, against 196 of 533 members. Horizon’s own page says no single funder provides a majority of its money.

People cross the other way, too.

Where the 29 placements were: 20 offices, committees and commissions

As the programme’s roster lists them, with the year each placement began (one has no year on the roster, and one host has since left Congress). The nine serving hosts who have also received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC received $608K in all; the first placement began in an earlier year than the first such gift for six of them, in the same year for one, in a later year for one, and is undated for one. No gift is tied to a placement. Fellows are counted, not named.

IV · The decade before

64 people went from Congress to jobs or advisory roles with the network or its lobbying firms.

Of the 64, 34 became lobbyists at firms that work for network clients and 30 joined the network’s own organisations, nine of them on advisory councils or boards, not in jobs. The 26 who came the other way are all Horizon fellows.

Each dot is one person. The gold line is the door: Congress on one side, the network on the other.

Source: House and Senate payroll reports, fellowship pages, lobbyists’ disclosed former posts and organisations’ staff pages.

Taking a job or a seat is not evidence about the work done in it. Each person counts once per direction.

Grants, hearings, fellows, jobs, money. Add it up.

V · The sum

Seventeen of the 533 members are tied six ways or more, counting what third parties did.

Each way is one kind of record. Eleven of the seventeen are Democrats and six are Republicans; Ted Lieu and Martin Heinrich are tied seven ways, and no one more.

Each kind of record counts once, however many records or dollars it holds.

Source: every record counted as evidence in this project’s tables and linked to a member serving on Nov. 26, 2026; activity through Sept. 30, 2026.

Breadth is not weight, and a tie can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. A blank means no counted record was found, not that none exists. Counting only records of what the network or the member did, one member is tied six ways (Ted Lieu).

And the other 433?

The nine kinds in the chart, and the seventeen members under each

A filled dot is a record on file. A ring is a record of what third parties did. A faint dot means no counted record was found, not that none exists.

V · The sum

239 of the 450 are tied only one or two ways. For 118, the only records are of what third parties did.

Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. One or two ways does not mean small sums: Thom Tillis is tied one way, $42.1M of super PAC spending against him.

Each dot is one of the 533 members, in the column for the number of kinds of record on file. A ring: only records of what third parties did.

Source: the record’s member table; 11 kinds of record, two of them records of what third parties did (lobbyists’ own gifts, super PAC spending).

The record shows the network money the super PACs received and the super PACs’ spending separately; it does not trace one to the other. Outside spending is not coordination with the candidate, and a lobbyist’s gift is the lobbyist’s own money.

So what does the whole record show?

V · The sum

A record of ties, not a record of influence.

The opening slide’s 533 seats again, by party. A ring is a member whose only records are of what third parties did: 40 of the 221 Democrats with a tie, 78 of the 226 Republicans.

Members serving on Nov. 26, 2026; records through Sept. 30, 2026.

The method: what counts as a tie, kind by kind, and what the record is made of

A tie is a record counted as evidence that links a member and the network. Activity stops at Sept. 30, 2026, and independent audits of the latest update were still open on Nov. 26, 2026. The 29 source figures, the tables and the method are in the repository.
